facts.text: Melvil Dewey was born on December 10, 1851, in Adams Center, New York.
Dewey entered Amherst College in the fall of 1870 and graduated with the class of 1874.
While a student working in the Amherst College library, Dewey presented the library committee on May 8, 1873, with a plan to rearrange its badly disorganized collection by subject.
Dewey was 21 years old when he presented his plan in May 1873.
Dewey said he visited over 50 libraries and was shocked by the time and money wasted on constantly recataloguing and renumbering books.
Most libraries of the time used a fixed system: a book's number showed the room, case or tier, and shelf where it happened to stand, not the subject it was about.

Other libraries of the 1800s shelved books in the order they arrived, or by size only; at Columbia, books of the same size were shelved together, so a reader might have to scan every book of the right size.
Under fixed systems, once the space for a subject filled up, books had to be moved and their numbers changed.
Dewey later wrote that the solution came to him one Sunday during a long sermon by the college president, Stearns, when he almost jumped up and shouted Eureka.
His idea was to number subjects, not shelves, using ordinary Arabic numerals as decimals to classify all printed knowledge.
In Dewey's system a book's number reflects its subject and shows only where the book stands relative to other books, so new books can be added without renumbering the old ones.
The first edition, published without the author's name in 1876, had ten main classes, each split into ten divisions and each division into ten sections: 1,000 categories in all.
The 1876 first edition ran to fewer than fifty pages.
Many librarians were at first overwhelmed by the 1,000 categories and called the scheme too detailed for libraries.
Because the numbers work as decimals, there is no limit to subdivision: no whole number fits between 356 and 357, but endless numbers fit between .356 and .357, so new subjects get longer numbers.
Because the system uses only Arabic numerals, the same number stands for the same subject in libraries using any language.
Dewey biographer Wayne Wiegand argues that Dewey joined and adjusted strong points from earlier schemes by others rather than creating something entirely new.
After graduating, Dewey worked as Amherst's assistant librarian until 1876, put his system into use there, sought a copyright for it, and helped found the American Library Association in 1876.
Dewey was a champion of spelling reform and dropped the extra letters from his first name, Melville.

Today Dewey's system is more common in public and school libraries, while the Library of Congress Classification is more common in large university and research libraries; the Library of Congress does not shelve its own books by Dewey.
Liu Guojun's Chinese library classification, first drafted in 1929, drew on old Chinese catalogues and on Dewey's system; it uses only numbers, with ten main classes expanded decimally.
In 1964 Lai Yung-hsiang revised Liu's scheme in Taiwan, keeping its ten main classes and adding categories for Taiwan.

Taiwan's National Central Library finished a revised version of the scheme in 2007 after six years of work, renaming it 中文圖書分類法; the revision consulted the Dewey Decimal Classification among other schemes.
The 23rd edition of the Dewey Decimal Classification was printed in 2011 in four volumes.
